newsitem.title: USA: Fake fencing scam at JFK Airport ends in arrests.
newsitem.headline: Fake fencing scam at JFK Airport ends in arrests.

text.p: An undercover fencing operation near John F. Kennedy International Airport ended on Wednesday with the arrest of 55 suspects who allegedly sold stolen cargoes ranging from airplane parts to designer clothes.

In the nearly 4-year-long sting operation, investigators said they bought $13 million worth of hot merchandise from truckers, importers, airline employees and suspected associates of New York's Gambino and Bonanno crime families.
State, local and federal officials took over an existing trucking and warehouse operation just outside the airport and spread the word they were in the market for stolen goods.
"JFK has been referred to as the mob's private candy store, but this case is much more than that," said Queens District Attorney Richard Brown, whose office is prosecuting about half the cases.

Through hundreds of unrelated schemes, airport cargoes were allegedly stolen from warehouses, hijacked from trucks at gunpoint or taken by airline workers and sold to undercover agents of the FBI and New York and New Jersey officers.
About 500 law enforcement personnel made 55 early morning arrests on Wednesday and the outcome of the New York dragnet was revealed at an afternoon news conference.
Another 20 suspects were arrested earlier and six others were still at large, investigators said.
Investigators said they paid only about $1 million for the stolen goods, a fraction of its wholesale value, including purchase of at least $3 million worth of airplane parts.

Other loot included 70 guns ranging from 9 mm pistols to AK 47 rifles, $500,000 worth of Waterford crystal, $400,000 in watches, $500,000 of Liz Claiborne clothes and, in the largest single transaction, $500,000 worth of Sony camcorders.
The case began when Port Authority detectives were probing stolen airplane parts, most of them taken from Continental Airlines and Pan Am inventories at the airport.

In one case, investigators tracked a shipment of 74 cashmere coats meant for Sak's Fifth Avenue through a trucking company identified as Powerhouse Trucking. Authorities said an associate of the Gambino family, Donna de Fillippo of Long Island, 42, helped arrange the coat sale.

In another case, a painting by artist Robert Motherwell which was valued at $100,000 was offered for $30,000 by a British Airways cargo worker and James LaRuffa, 46, allegedly an associate of the Bonanno crime family, officials said. The painting had been missing since 1977 from West Germany.
